title: Ojibwe and D(L)akota native star maps as astronomically accurate artworks communicating an indigenous perspective of the night sky
description: Two native star maps created in 2012 are the foundation of the initiative's work: the Ojibwe Giizhiig Anung Masinaaigan, painted by the author and William Wilson based on Carl Gawboy's unpublished research, and the D(L)akota Makoċe Wiċaŋḣpi Wowapi, painted by the author with language expert Jim Rock based on Ron Goodman's published work. The article states the maps are "astronomically accurate and visual works of art created to communicate an indigenous perspective of the night sky." Both center on the north celestial pole and North Star, with seasonal stars arranged around the center and Greek constellations lightly painted for common ground.
requirements: Created collaboratively by native-led teams of artists, astronomers, and language and cultural experts, since no one person holds all of the star knowledge
constraints: Designed for a viewing location of approximately 40-50 degrees north latitude
target_learning_goals: Ojibwe and D(L)akota constellations and star knowledge
cultural connections to the night sky
examples: The Ojibwe map was painted in a traditional woodland x-ray style by Wilson; the Dakota map in a pointillist style suggesting beadwork

title: Ojibwe and D(L)akota planispheres as tangible manipulatives for learning night-sky patterns
description: The initiative produced planispheres, two-dimensional versions of astrolabes consisting of an inner year-round star map circle and an outer holder, letting a user get a snapshot view of the sky for any time and date and watch how the sky changes. The article asserts that "Tangible resources are essential when working to engage communities in learning the patterns of the night sky." The outer perimeter carries native month names tied to the Moon and cultural events, and a blank star circle without constellation lines supports practicing the visual patterns.
requirements: Tangible manipulatives to engage communities in learning night-sky patterns
constraints: Accurate for latitudes 40-50 degrees N and the current epoch of Polaris; precession would shift the view over longer time periods; month names vary with local latitude and longitude
target_learners: community members learning the night sky
target_learning_goals: patterns of constellations in the night sky
seasonal month names and cultural events
examples: August is Manoominike-giizis (Ricing Moon) in Ojibwe and March is Iṡta Wicayazaŋ Wi (Sore Eyes Moon) in Dakota on the planisphere rims
